content.content:
1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
120

1	# Keeping the record
2	
3	How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.
4	
5	**history**
6	: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.
7	
8	**pointer**
9	: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."
10	
11	**pass**
12	: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.
13	
14	## What an entry is
15	
16	An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17	
18	- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19	- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
20	- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
21	- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
22	- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it. If the choice is consequential, its review-queue item names that entry.
23	- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
24	- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
25	- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
26	- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
27	- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
28	- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
29	- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
30	- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
31	- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
32	- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
33	
34	Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
35	
36	1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
37	2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
38	3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
39	4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
40	5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
41	6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
42	
43	In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:
44	
45	- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
46	- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
47	- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
48	- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
49	- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
50	- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.
51	
52	An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:
53	
54	- keep: every check passes;
55	- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
56	- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
57	- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.
58	
59	Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.
60	
61	## Reading and writing
62	
63	- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
64	- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
65	- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
66	- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
67	- Commit the record file and its history together.
68	- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
69	- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.
70	
71	## The pass
72	
73	Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.
74	
75	The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.
76	
77	1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
78	2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
79	3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
80	   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
81	   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
82	   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
83	4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
84	5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.
85	
86	Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.
87	
88	## A consolidation
89	
90	A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").
91	
92	- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
93	- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
94	- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
95	- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
96	- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
97	- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
98	- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.
99	
100	## The consolidation tools
101	
102	Four Workflow scripts keep the record and the worker skill current and readable. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Give a run only its arguments and the input files that its README names. Add no rules of your own over the tool's briefs, and change the briefs only where its README says to, such as their paths. If the briefs do not fit the job, propose their change to the curator. Decide the open questions of the runs as any decision: only a consequential one goes in the review queue.
103	
104	Pick the tool by the job:
105	
106	- To bring the record in line with a landing: the record-landing workflow (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"). Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`.
107	- To find whether a POSITIONS entry comes from the curator's words or from an agent's summary or default: the mining workflow. Its writer changes only a sentence that is false, stale or not the curator's. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
108	- To make entries read on their own, with their meaning kept: the clarity workflow. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is", and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
109	- To correct the entries that a review's findings name: the clarity workflow, with `findings.md` in each chunk's folder, in the form that its README gives. An entry changes only where a finding names it, and grows only by what the correction needs.
110	- To keep `fortress-repo`'s revival part short enough to read whole: the orientation workflow. Its update mode runs after each landing. Run its consolidate mode when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`.
111	
112	## INDEX and the gap ledger
113	
114	- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
115	- Put a run's working files in an `evidence/` folder beside its results file: its briefs, chunks and checks, and the worker reports that the results draw on. Move them there with `git mv` once the results are judged. Only the results file gets an INDEX line. `check-index.sh` skips evidence folders. Do not add a folder's name to its list to let the folder pass.
116	- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
117	- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.

6	
7	Terms. A **chunk**: 19 to 42 entries of one section. A **scout**: a Sonnet agent that only gathers. A **writer**: an Opus agent that rewrites one chunk. ### Worked examples

Five entries of the trial (Part 3) and of the pairs (Part 3b), rewritten to "What an entry is". Each gives the old text, the new text, and the question that decided each cut or keep. An entry's number is its line in `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md` today, which the record store's design makes its number. A pointer is the target's number in the sentence that needs it, as the reviewed design has it (`record-store-review.md`, section 3). Two old texts are long, so only their start is quoted and the rest is listed in brackets. P-48's old text is the one on `main` today. Sizes are characters of the entry's line. A brief may quote the new texts and their notes without the old texts.

The five new texts come to 3,086 characters against 17,952, 17 %. Four are under 600 characters. F-58 passes that measure, for the reason that its notes give.

#### F-58: the errors by kind, not a bare count

Old, 3,200 characters:

> - **MicroGPT's own programs through the compiled checker against the one library: none of their errors is a numeral, the model's unsized array types are the largest part, and every count is a floor** (`reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 2; `reviews/numerics-plan-fable.md` sections 3.2 and 3.6; `reviews/numerics-plan-synthesis.md` section 7). C4's own errors are 26. 15 are decision D, the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` where the library's `DOT`, `gather`, `row`, `plane`, `parseRow` and the `reflect` views want `Vector`, `Matrix` or `Array3`: the four row lifts, `plane` and the three `reflect` bridges in `FlatArrays`, `parseRow` twice in `FlatData`, `gather` twice and `DOT` three times in the model. 5 are numeral powers that the checker's coercion attempt refuses as an ambiguous coercion, `10.0^(-5)` on the hyperparameter line (its second power, `10.0^(-8)`, not reached), `10.0^10` in the mask and the check program's three tolerances, since `RR64`'s `^` on an `RR64` and `MultiplicativeRing`'s `^` on a `ZZ64` both apply only by converting the integer (row 533; walk takes them). 6 are small: `Character.codePoint`, `diag`'s body an `Array2` against a declared `Matrix`, a varargs `SUM[\ZZ32\][m <- ms]` typed at the element, the varargs export, `matShape`'s `if` body typed `((), ())` (row 474), `view`'s arity. With decision D's diff (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md`; the model 21 lines out and 29 in), C4's own errors are 14: all 15 of decision D gone as such; 3 `DOT`s failing on the library api's dead sizes (decision E's E3), the `adam` bridge, `numbersOf`'s discarded count, the 5 powers and 4 small items. 58:## The checker count and the distance
59-
60:Until the switch-over lands, the gate of every batch reports the checker count and the distance. Neither turns the gate red.
61-
62-- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
63-- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
64-- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
65-- The post-batch review lists each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.
66-
67-## Reserved points and repairs
68-
69-- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default. If the point is consequential, such as a line of microGPT, its question also goes in the review queue. A point that is no decision, such as an output that a rung cannot explain, becomes a ledger row.
70-- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
71-- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Give its findings to the post-batch reviewer ("The landing", step 3). The reviewer puts them in its list for the batch after: the part of its review that the next planner reads. The review runs once in each batch.
72-- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
73-- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.
74-
75-## While it runs
76-
77-- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
78-- The rungs, their skeptics and their judges work in their own worktrees, and do not read the main tree. The gather and the stages after it work there, and the gather needs `git status --porcelain` to print nothing. So until the gather starts, commit in the main tree as usual, by named paths, and push at once. From the gather's start until the batch's push, change nothing there, the boot note included: a compaction ask waits for the push. Keep `origin/main` at or behind the main tree's head, or git refuses the commit stage's push. So push `main` from no other tree. From the main tree, push nothing that the batch committed: the commit stage pushes it.
79-- Before the launch, name the check-in file in the boot note: `<scratchpad>/batch<N>/checkins.txt`, where `<N>` is the batch's number. After the launch, write the run's ID and each armed check-in's ID in that file. If the scratchpad loses a check-in's ID, find the check-in again with `list_triggers`.
80-- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
81-- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.
82-
83-## The landing
84-
85-The landing check is `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, run by the gather and by the merged-diff review on the batch's base. It reports a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test removed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status. A finding the base already had counts too. The gather clears each finding before its commit, through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or by a reworded entry. The merged-diff review clears any that is left in its corrections commit. So a batch lands only when the check prints nothing.
86-
87-The batch workflow holds the push when a point to report still acts against a decision on record after the repairs. Its result then gives `pushHeld` true, and `heldBy` lists the points. If the batch's push is held for the curator, take steps 1 to 3 at once on the local commits. Only these wait: the push, the parts of step 3's routing check that need the pushed hashes, and step 4, since the record-landing workflow pushes `main` itself. If `heldBy` names either of these, push only after the curator's go:
88-
89-- a step that cannot be undone;
90-- a change that still acts against the curator's word.

F-53 gives the last gate's total. That gate's `distance.txt` reads '#crash none': the checker checks `value object Char` to its end (F-334), and the `FortressLibrary` component to its end too (F-233). FACTS.md:133

Both are in the distance stage's list (`tools/distance/run.sh:87-90`), and both import nothing. Over the fourteen, the stage reads '#total 0' and '#crash none' (F-54). `CovariantCollection`'s api states its component's members and headers, and its `upward` takes its target type from its first argument. The export check matches an object's value parameter by its modifiers other than `var` and its type, not by its name (row 839). Every `ArrayList` holds `OneShot` fields (`List.fss:253-254`) and every list comprehension goes through `covariantCompr` (`List.fss:178-179`), so after the switch-over `List` compiles only with both (the distance measures the checker, not the code generator). POSITIONS.md:38
- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. Until the switch-over lands, every batch's gate also measures the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component (F-53), so a native binding moved onto a helper in another component is checked by the distance alone, and P-58 has each moved binding checked from the step that moves it.

# Rung G of climb batch 17: walk's load check reads every pair of generic declarations by the checker's rules

- problem: walk refused two generic functions unless a parameter pair excluded (row 159, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:299`), and loaded two declarations whose declared domains are equal (rows 742 and 549, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:351`, `:340`); the five tests of section 2 were red on the base through the harness.
- spec: `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-110` (a declaration with static parameters is read over its instances and compared on the parameter types it declares; the rules are in `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:531-575`, "Declarations with Static Parameters").
- precedent: `genericPairValid`, climb batch 16's reading of a withdrawn pair on its declared domains (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:844` after the skeptic's fix, `:842` at b5a497c04, at the base `:801`), and the generic-beside-plain branch of `validOnDeclaredDomains`, which refuses `plainInside && genInside` (at the base `:781-783`).
- deviation: the refusal of equal declared domains reads a pair that the parameter check passed, which no precedent reads, and gives the team's message for equal parameter lists (`OverloadedFunction.java:628`, the team's `:573` at `a874948ac`) for two lists that differ as written (`OverloadedFunction.java:533-540`).
- historical: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java`, `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex` (each a file of the 2012 tree; every line changed in them is the revival's).

## 1. What changed and why

P-45 decides that walk's load check reads every pair of generic declarations on their declared domains by the checker's rules, with no parameter pair required to exclude (row 159). Climb batch 16 built that reading only for a pair some parameter pair of which had excluded in walk's reading of each at a symbolic instantiation and then had the exclusion withdrawn (F-238). This rung widens it to every pair, and adds the No Duplicates Rule for the pairs that the parameter check orders wrongly (rows 742 and 549).

In `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java` (commit `b5a497c04`):

- `validOnDeclaredDomains` (`:750-793`) reads a pair of two own generics that the parameter check refuses by `genericPairValid` whether or not an exclusion was withdrawn: `return genericPairValid(o1, o2, all);` (`:766`) in place of `return withdrawn && genericPairValid(o1, o2, all);`. `genericPairValid` (`:842` at b5a497c04) is unchanged: refused where each declared domain lies inside the other (No Duplicates), valid where one lies inside the other and its return type is below at the holding instance (Return Type), else valid where a third declaration below both holds the overlap (`genericMeetCovered`, Meet).
- `completeOverloadingCheck` (`:528-540`): a pair that the check passes without an excluding parameter is read again by `sameDeclaredDomains` (`:795-822`, with `declaredInside`, `:824-832`): where one at least is an own generic and the other an own generic or a declaration without static parameters, and each declared domain lies inside the other (each generic's over its own instances, by `instanceHolding`), the pair is refused, "Overloading of ... and ... fails because their parameter lists have the same types". The parameter check reads a type parameter `T` as strictly below its bound `Wide` and sets `p1better`, so it orders `tie[\T extends Wide\](a: T, b: T)` before `tie(a: Wide, b: Wide)` or `tie[\T extends Wide\](a: Wide, b: Wide)`, though at the bound the two declared domains are one.
- The `withdrawn` field, its reset and its one assignment go, since nothing reads it now (at the base `:310-312`, `:340`, `:479`).
- The two comments that climb batch 16's judge left (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-16/JUDGE-review.md:136-138`) read F-238's reading: the loop's comment (`:464-466`), "Read each at a symbolic instantiation of its static parameters, shared where both declare the same ones", and `validOnDeclaredDomains`'s comment (`:757-761`), which now says that every refused pair of two own generics is read on its declared domains. The field's comment (at the base `:310-311`) went with the field.

The object-type shortcut (`:437-443`, `:509`, row 697's) and rung W's `bestMatchWithCoercion` and `bestMatchInternal` are untouched; a three-way merge with `origin/wip/rung-walk-method-sargs` is clean (`git merge-tree --write-tree HEAD origin/wip/rung-walk-method-sargs` exits 0).

The specification's two revival sentences on these rows are edited (section 4).

======
## 5. Old against new

Each program run under walk from the rung's scratch folder, new with `bin/fortress`, old with `old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base17 <tree>/tmp/old-caches` (or an empty private folder where a cold cache is named):

| program | base | this tree |
|---|---|---|
| `which`/`ident`, nested bounds (`GenericPairNestedBoundsWalk`) | refused, 'at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types' | loads; `round`, `shape`; `ident` returns its argument |

## 1. What changed and why

### Row 373: two generic declarations, each read over its own instances

Walk's load check compares each pair of overloads parameter by parameter (`OverloadComparisonResult.completeOverloadingCheck`). For two declarations with static parameters of their own it read both domains at one instantiation in two ways, both the team's:

- Two generic functions of one name and one list of static parameters (names, kinds, bounds) share one symbolic instantiation (`FGenericFunction.java:43-64`, keyed by `GenericComparer`, `GenericFunctionOrMethod.java:43-68`). So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\])` read `P[\T\]` and `Q[\T\]` at one `T`, where `trait P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }` makes them exclude (`OverloadedFunction.java:454` on the base), though `Mixed extends { P[\ZZ32\], Q[\String\] }` has both.
- Two instances of one generic object at different symbolic static arguments, `ListI[\P\]` beside `ListI[\Q\]` or `Box[\T\]` beside `Box[\U\]`, are two object types that cannot be extended, so they exclude (`interpreter/evaluator/types/FType.java:212-217`), and every differing parameter being an object type marks the pair distinct anyway (the shortcut, `OverloadedFunction.java:432-433` and `:486` on the base). So A6's two `sort`s and B4's two `dup`s loaded.

Now, for two own generics (`ownGeneric` of both, `OverloadedFunction.java:424`):

- A parameter pair the old reading finds excluding is read again over the instances of each (`excludesOverInstances`, `:1059-1067`), o2's static parameters renamed apart from o1's where the two share their symbolic instantiation (`Apart`, `:1006-1032`, made with `createSymbolicInstantiation` and `typeApply`). Instances of one generic type exclude only where their static arguments cannot be equal (`mayBeEqual`, `:1133-1148`: two type parameters unless their bounds exclude, a type parameter and a type within its bounds, one generic's instances argument by argument). Any other pair excludes as `excludesOther` reads it apart, or, read at the shared instantiation, where every generic type both extend forces o2's renamed static arguments back to the shared ones (`oneInstance`, `:1077-1092`): no type extends two instances of one generic trait, so `Array[\T,ZZ32\]` beside `ImmutableArray[\T,ZZ32\]`, which exclude at one `T` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1455`), exclude at every pair of instances through `ReadableArray`. Where it does not hold, the exclusion is withdrawn (`:467-479`).
- A coinciding pair of one generic object's instances is no object type for the shortcut (`:443-446`); the shortcut itself (`:513`) is the team's line, unchanged.
- A withdrawn position counts as one with generic type (`:499-501`), so a refusal keeps walk's generic message, "with generic type, at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types" (F-155).
- A pair with a withdrawn exclusion that the check then refuses is read on its declared domains, each over its own instances (`validOnDeclaredDomains`, `:764`; `genericPairValid`, `:801-818`): each inside the other is refused (the No Duplicates Rule); one inside the other is valid where its return type is below the other's at the instance that holds it (the Return Type Rule); otherwise a third declaration whose declared domain lies inside both must hold their overlap (`genericMeetCovered`, `:833-878`, the Meet Rule). The overlap matches the two domains position by position (`matchApart`, `:969-988`); type parameters matched to each other become one made afresh whose bounds are each one's, evaluated in an environment where each declaration's static parameters stand for their arguments at the overlap, as `createSymbolicInstantiation` evaluates bounds, so F-bounds meet (`meetParams`, `:891-961`).

Pairs that the old reading did not find excluding keep the old check (`:764` returns false without a withdrawal): row 159's renamed and swapped arms stay refused, and `XXXDispatchRenamedArmWalkRungG` and `XXXDispatchSwappedArmWalkRungG` keep their verdicts.

## 9. Decisions

1. **How far row 373 reaches.** Chosen: a pair of two own generics is read over the instances of each only where a parameter pair excluded read at one instantiation and does not read apart; such a pair is then judged on its declared domains by the three rules. Not taken: reading every pair of two generic declarations on its declared domains, as the checker does, which would also accept row 159's renamed and swapped arms, turning `XXXDispatchRenamedArmWalkRungG` and `XXXDispatchSwappedArmWalkRungG` red, a design limit the record keeps (row 159, "walk's check is kept by decision"); only renaming the static parameters apart at the exclusion test (`:454` on the base), which leaves A6 and B4 loading, since their declarations share no instantiation and walk took their instances of one object as distinct non-extensible types (`FType.java:212-217`) and through the shortcut; giving each generic its own symbolic instantiation in `FGenericFunction.getSymbolic` (`FGenericFunction.java:43-64`), which changes every generic's domain for dispatch and inference as well, and is a fourth file. Evidence: the failing run of section 2; row 159's tests in the passing run. Question for the curator: `record.md`.
2. **The object shortcut.** Chosen: instances of one generic object whose static arguments may be equal count as no object type (`:443-446`). Not taken: dropping the shortcut for two own generics, which would repair row 697 for generic pairs with a ground object type below the other's, beyond the rung and against the record's reading of row 697 (its repair waits on row 433); leaving it, which keeps A6 and B4 loading. Evidence: A6 and B4 have one parameter each, both instances of one object, so the shortcut alone marks them distinct (`:486` on the base).
3. **An exclusion read at one shared instantiation, of two different generic types.** Chosen: it stands where every generic type both extend forces the renamed static arguments back to the shared ones, the instantiation exclusion of `advanced/overloading.tex:584-588` (`oneInstance`). Not taken: withdrawing every such exclusion, which refused `Library/Shuffle.fss:21` beside `:30` (section 5); keeping every one, which loads row 373's own program. Evidence: `GenericPairExcludingWalk`'s `copyOf` pair and `GenericOverloadInstancesApartWalk`.
4. **The overlap of two generic domains.** Chosen: matched position by position, with a type parameter made afresh under the bounds of each, evaluated from the declarations as `createSymbolicInstantiation` evaluates them, and covered by a third declaration whose declared domain lies inside both and holds the overlap (`advanced/overloading.tex:553-555`). Not taken: joining the bounds as run-time types, which gave up on a bound that names a static parameter and refused `GenericFBoundsMeetWalk`'s valid set (section 5); building the overlap by substitution inside run-time types, which needs the bound of a type parameter not yet made; no cover at all, which turns `GenericBoundsMeetWalk` red. A pair whose domains do not match so (a lone type parameter against a parameterized type, a tuple or an arrow over static parameters) or that has a `where` clause is refused, as walk refused every such pair whose parameters did not exclude before.
5. **The Return Type Rule of a nested pair.** Chosen: the inner declaration's return type below the outer's at the instance of the outer that holds the inner's domain, as the checker's `satisfiesReturnTypeRule` solves the outer's static parameters (`scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:83-128`). Not taken: comparing the two symbolic return types, as the generic-beside-plain path does (`OverloadedFunction.java:784-785`), which for two generics compares types over unrelated static parameters.
6. **The message.** Chosen: a withdrawn position counts as one with generic type, so the refusal is walk's generic message, the key of the two promoted tests and F-155's. Not taken: a new message, which would change both tests' keys.
7. **How `forIf` knows a `Maybe`.** Chosen: by its type, named `Just` or `Nothing` and extending the library's `Maybe` (`Glue.extendsGenericTrait`, as `Evaluator.java:416` reads `Contains`), a `Just` true whatever it holds. Not taken: calling the `holds` getter, Fortress code run from inside `forIf`, which the coordinator's call allows equally; the team's name test alone, which takes any object named `Just`, a program's own among them; constants in `compiler/WellKnownNames.java`, a fourth file. Evidence: `maybeTest` and `naturalsTest` green; `IfClauseObjectWalk`, `IfClauseNumberWalk`, `IfClauseStringWalk`.
8. **How `resultArgOf` reaches the supertype.** Chosen: the declaration's extends clause as written, its static parameters replaced by the declared result's static arguments with the checker's `StaticTypeReplacer`, up the supertypes, at most 16 deep. Not taken: the run-time supertypes of an instance (`getTransitiveExtends`), which are run-time types where the unification needs the written type that names the operator's own static parameters; a substitution visitor of walk's own, which repeats the checker's; one level only, which misses a trait that extends `BigOperator` through another.
9. **Tests.** Chosen: the number and the string in two files, since a refusal at load stops at its first; row 373's own program as a gated test; two guards green on the base and after. Not taken: one file with both, which can assert only one.
10. **The specification.** Chosen: no edit; the four clauses and the fifth sentence go to the gather with their corrected text, as the brief says.

## What changed and why

Under `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` no compile wrote the one library's jars: the wrapper generator found no converter for the one library's `String` at a helper's Java `String` (row 874), and nothing carried its built-in types at run (row 1062). The rung builds the decisions on record: each number type a value object over a payload class (P-178, fork N4), `Boolean`, `Char` and `FlatString` in the same form (fork C1), the reader, the writer and the two stores as classes of the one library's traits (P-164, P-169), and one build for both libraries, the one library's classes in a second folder first on the class path (P-33, F-353, fork C2). From the planner's patch (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-34/probes/rehearsal-34.patch`) it took by hand the carriers, the tables, the converters, the names and the classes, and none of its stand-ins in the library's text or `OverloadSet.java`.

## The design as built (a point to report)

- **The second set and how the class path chooses it.** `ProjectFortress/src-one` holds `FBoolean`, `FCharacter`, `FJavaString` (payload classes over `boolean`, `int`, `String`), `FJavaBufferedReader`, `FJavaBufferedWriter`, `FJavaArrayStore`, `FJavaRR64ArrayStore` (each over the one library's trait, its Java value in a field), `FValue`, `MutableFValue` and `FException` (the first set's, `asString` typed at `FValue`), `LibraryNames`, and `fortress/FortressLibrary.java`, a stub of the four traits that those classes extend. `ant compileAll` compiles it into `ProjectFortress/build-one` after the first set, and whole again when the first set changed (`build.xml:853-872`); the stamp of the implementation and the sources' fingerprint cover both folders (`build.xml:402`, the two macros), and `ant clean` deletes it. `bin/fortress_classpath:27-39` puts `build-one` before `build` where `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, so the compile, the run (`bin/run_classpath` builds on it) and `junit.sh` pick it; the onelibrary track's JVM takes it by `fastTrack`'s new attribute `classesFirst` (`build.xml:1236-1251`, `:1180`, `:1310`). At a run the jars come first (`bin/run_classpath`), so the stub's classes give way to `FortressLibrary`'s.
- **The payload table's rows** (`NamingCzar.java:637-655`): the prelude's seven as before, and `FortressLibrary`'s `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64`, `RR64`, `FortressBuiltin`'s `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` (payload `Z`), `Char` (`I`), and `FlatString`'s `FlatString` (`Ljava/lang/String;`). A lookup answers only a row of the library that the compile reads, FlatString counted as one of the one library's apis under the selection (`:661-675`).
- **The carried types' rows** (`NamingCzar.java:612-624`): under the selection only, since each row also enters the bare name: `FortressLibrary`'s five numbers, `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaBufferedWriter`, `JavaArrayStore`, `JavaRR64ArrayStore`, `FortressBuiltin`'s `Char` and `FlatString`'s `FlatString` (`Boolean`, `NN32`, `RR32` are `fortLib`'s rows there). The run's copy is `runtimeSystem/Naming.java:307-322`, keyed by library. A carried parent of an `extends` clause is named by its interface (`NamingCzar.java:911`), for `FortressBuiltin`'s private objects below `JavaArrayStore` and `JavaBufferedReader`.
- **The names that the second set's LibraryNames gives** (`ProjectFortress/src-one/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/LibraryNames.java`): `fortress.FortressBuiltin$NN32`, `$RR32`, `$Boolean`, `$Char`; `FlatString$FlatString`; `fortress.FortressLibrary$ZZ32`, `$ZZ64`, `$ZZ`, `$NN64`, `$RR64`; an exception `fortress.FortressLibrary$<name>`; the library's String `fortress.FortressLibrary$String`. The first set's copy names the prelude (`fortress.CompilerBuiltin$`, `FailCalled` `fortress.CompilerLibrary$`) and answers no number class where the one library is selected, as before. Both reach a class through `LibraryObjects` (new, first set), the reflection that `LibraryNames` held.
- **The converters** (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java:77-109`, `:191-198`): a helper's Java `String` at the one library's `String` is cast to `FJavaString` and unwrapped, a result made by `FJavaString.make`; a Java `Object` at `Any` passes as it is, cast to `fortress/AnyType$Any` on the way out; `FJavaArrayStore` and `FJavaRR64ArrayStore` convert as the readers do.
- **The raise strings.** 99 strings name an exception by its simple name: 87 raises and `FAIL_CALLED` (`nativeHelpers/runtime.java:29`) in `nativeHelpers/`, 11 raises in `FortressBufferedReader` and `FortressBufferedWriter`. `Utility.makeFortressException` (`Utility.java:28-69`) maps a simple name through the set's `LibraryNames` (a whole class name passes as it is), looks up the constructor over the library's `String` by name, and for an object without one, as the one library's `IOFailure` and `FileNotFoundException` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2064-2070`), the constructor without parameters. A class not found still raises `FortressImplementationError` with the class name, which walk reads (`interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java:273-282`).
- **Each place that names a prelude class at run.** In the second set: none (`grep -rn 'CompilerBuiltin\|CompilerLibrary' ProjectFortress/src-one` prints nothing). In the first set, which both libraries run: the seven payload classes' `asString` bridges, typed at the prelude's `String` (the bridge of `FZZ32.asString`, `FZZ32.java:27`), and the first set's `LibraryNames` (`PRELUDE_CLASS_PREFIX`). The first set's `FBoolean`, `FCharacter`, `FJavaString`, `FJavaBufferedReader`, `FJavaBufferedWriter`, `FString`, `FZZ32Vector`, `FStringVector`, `FValue`, `MutableFValue` and `FException` are the prelude's own, which the second set shadows.

====
## What changed and why

**Row 994.** `OverloadSet` named the owner of a generic overloaded function's instance table, and its template class, by the api's bare name at four places, `Naming.dotToSep(f.tagA.getText())`, where every other place asks `NamingCzar.javaPackageClassForApi`, which puts a default library's classes in the package `fortress`. The four now ask it (fork C1, the rehearsal's W11): `generateClosureTableOwner` (`OverloadSet.java:962`), `invokeArmAtTemplateParams` (`:1421`), and the two template names of `generateCall` (`:1784`, `:1788`). No bare api name is left in `OverloadSet.java`; `Naming.dotToSep` in `CodeGen.java:6412` names a payload class, not an api. A program's own component is not a default library's, so its names do not change.

**Rows 1091 and 1099.** The code generator could write a method twice into one class, under one name and descriptor; the JVM refuses such a class as it loads. An instrumented copy of `ManglingClassWriter` (in `tmp/`, never in the tree) that reported every second method of a name and descriptor, over a compile of the one library's `AnyType`, `FortressBuiltin`, `FortressLibrary`, `RangeInternals` and `List` on the base's code, found four shapes:

- a trait's own forwarder beside a narrowing bridge from a generic trait at its own type (`ImmutableArray1`'s `copy`, `tabulate`, `fill`; `Array1`, `Array2` and `Array3`'s `copy`; `Vector`'s and `Matrix`'s prefix `-`): first `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining:1679`, again `dumpMethodChaining:1124`;
- a trait's own forwarder beside a dispatch method among the trait's and its generic parent's declarations (`Vector`'s and `Matrix`'s `+` and `-`): first `generateTopLevelOverloads:8823` from `forTraitDecl`, again `dumpMethodChaining:1124`; the dispatch's two branches both called the interface's method of its own name and descriptor;
- one narrowing bridge for each of two parents that give the same (`FullScalarRange`'s, `FullRange2D`'s and `FullRange3D`'s `narrowToRange`; the object `SimpleSeqFilterGenerator`'s `seq`): both `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining:1679`;
- an inherited body's forwarder beside the class's own method at the same descriptor (`List`'s `=`, and its name mangled away from overloading): first `dumpMethodChaining:1160`, again `:1124`; and in three objects a bridge beside the object's own method (`TransposedArray2`'s `replica` and `t`, `TransposedMatrix`'s `t` and `scale`).

A scan of every class file in the jars for a method held twice by name and descriptor counts them:

    python3 -I tmp/rung-one-library-run-walls/tools/dupscan.py tmp/rung-one-library-run-walls/old-one/bytecode_cache/*.jar      (the base's fourteen jars, the base build's caches-one)
    dupscan: 2208 classes, 25 methods held twice
    python3 -I tmp/rung-one-library-run-walls/tools/dupscan.py default_repository/caches-one/bytecode_cache/*.jar                 (the same fourteen, compiled by 7c7b040927's code)
    dupscan: 2208 classes, 0 methods held twice
    python3 -I tmp/rung-one-library-run-walls/tools/dupscan.py /home/user/fortress-wsuite/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/*.jar   (the prelude's, on the base)
    dupscan: 476 classes, 0 methods held twice

The repair (fork C2): `CodeGenClassWriter` keeps a record of the methods that a class gets, by name and descriptor, and the methods that the code generator writes between `startBridges` and `endBridges` are bridges: it holds each in an ASM `MethodNode` until the class ends (`visitEnd`), and writes it there only where the class has no method of its name and descriptor yet. So the class's own method is written over a bridge at its own signature, as `traits.tex:581-592` has a declaration of the type itself replace an inherited one at the same parameter types, and a bridge that two parents give is written once. Every other method is written as before, a second one of a name and descriptor included, so a defect of another kind still shows as it loads. `CodeGen` marks four places as bridges: in `forObjectDeclPrePass` (`CodeGen.java:5336-5345`) and `forTraitDecl` (`:6114-6125`), the call of `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining` and of `generateTopLevelOverloads` for the type's dispatch methods; in `dumpMethodChaining` (`:1160-1165`), the forwarders to an inherited body; and `overrideBridges` (`:1235-1244`). `visitMethod` and `visitCGMethod` of `CodeGenClassWriter` now reach `visitNoMangleMethod` by a virtual call, so that every method passes the record; a bridge's instructions are mangled as they are held and replayed into the class writer unchanged. The template of a generic trait holds the duplicate already, with its static parameters in the descriptor, so the record sees it there; two methods whose descriptors differ in the template and become equal only at an instance are not seen.

What it does not change: which declaration the code generator gathers, compares or bridges. The classification in `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining` that made a bridge or a dispatch at a descriptor where the type's own declaration replaces the inherited one (its domain and return comparisons over static parameters, and a trait's `T` substituted again in the target descriptor, as `ImmutableArray1`'s bridge to `copy()` answering `ImmutableArray1⟦ImmutableArray1⟦T,b0,s0⟧,b0,s0⟧`) is left as it is: those methods are now never written.

====
## Defects and their homes

- Row 994, the bare api name: home 1, `OneLibraryRunStringEquality.test` (and the `seq` of `OneLibraryArr`, `OneLibraryDot`, the `|xs|` of `OneLibraryVarargsArguments`).

content.content:
After the phases, each path has its own code for these:

- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`), payload classes, which hold the JVM value, as `FRR64` holds a `double`. The classes of the number objects of both compiled libraries, the prelude and the one library, extend them, and under the one library so do those of `Boolean`, `Char` and `FlatString`.
- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`ZZ32.java`, `ZZ64.java`).
- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.

Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.

The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, it uses the one library in their place. The runtime's classes that name a library's types, as `FValue`, `FException` and `LibraryNames`, come in two sets under the same names: one built from `ProjectFortress/src` into `ProjectFortress/build`, for the prelude, and one built from `ProjectFortress/src-one` into `ProjectFortress/build-one`, for the one library. `ant compileAll` builds both. With the variable, the class path puts the second set first. If you change a class that `src-one` also holds, make the same change to its copy there. `LibraryNames` gives the JVM names of its library's classes, as the class of an exception that a helper raises by its simple name. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: the switch-over deletes them, and their tests stay. Two exceptions (P-37): its numeral types and coercions follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", and its seven number types are each one `value object`, as in the interpreter's library. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even if the prelude binds it, and leave the prelude's text: its binding gives the fix. Change with it a compiled test that pinned the old result.

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `spawn`;
36:## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
37-
38:For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
39-
40-- `spawn`;
41-- an object expression;
42-- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`;
43-- a built-in number type named as a value, as `x: Object = ZZ32`: 'Can't compile the number type ZZ32 as a value yet' (ledger row 1082).
44-
45-Against the compiler's prelude, it refuses a varargs parameter: 'Can't compile VarArgs yet: the library in use, CompilerLibrary, declares no ImmutableArray, ...'. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, it compiles a varargs parameter. There it stops with `OptionUnwrapException` on a varargs method, or a generic varargs function, where another declaration of its name has the same number of parameters, the varargs parameter counted as one (ledger row 1086). Give the varargs declaration its own name.
46-
47-Against the one library, a compiled program fails where walk runs these constructs:
48-
49-- `println` of a number or a boolean: 'NoSuchMethodError' (ledger row 1098);
50-- `u.asString` in a generic body, for `u` of a type parameter bounded by `ZZ32`: 'NoSuchMethodError' (ledger row 1101);
51-- an uncaught exception: the run reports it with a placeholder, 'Bogus value from FValue.asString()', not with its `asString` (ledger row 1102).
52-
53-Write none of these in a one-library run test. A test of one is an `XXX` test that names its row (`tests-writing.md`).
54-
55-It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):
56-
57-- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
58-- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
59-- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.
60-
61-A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The chosen declaration is the one that the checker chooses at the assumed types. A dotted call's receiver is not one of its arguments. The code generator compiles an assumption in these places, and elsewhere as the value of `e`:
62-
63-- at a dotted call's receiver, `(r asif T).m(a)`, where every argument is an assumption or `T` has one method `m`;
--
118:To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. To test a binding of the one library, put the test in `one_library_tests/`, whose tests compile against the one library and run against its jars (`tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests"). Such a test can use none of the constructs that "What the compiled path cannot compile yet" lists.
119-
120-The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:
121-
122-- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
123-- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
124-- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
125-- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.
126-
127-The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these three types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.
128-
129-The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.
130-
131-## Traps of the compiled path
132-
133-- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
134-- Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `=/=` at `RR32` and `RR64`, so the checker refuses `r =/= 0` for an `RR64` value `r` (ledger row 1059). Write `NOT (r = 0)`. For an `RR32` value `c`, the checker refuses `c = 0`: 'Ambiguous coercion in call to operator ='. `c = d` for two `RR32` values compiles, and overflows the stack when it runs (ledger row 528). Bind `c` at `RR64` first, as `r: RR64 = c`, and compare `r`.
135-- A parameter of a declared tuple type is one JVM parameter for each element (F-378). So in a `VerifyError`, the method's descriptor lists each element of a tuple parameter as a parameter of its own. These three tuple forms fail:
136-  - an object's method overloaded at a pair and at another type fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 1054). Give the two methods two names;
137-  - an object whose one value parameter is a pair dies in its constructor with `ClassCastException` (ledger row 1055). Add a second value parameter beside the pair, as `object Holder(n: ZZ32, var pr: (ZZ32, ZZ32))`;
138-  - a generic operator whose one parameter has its type parameter's type, applied to a pair, dies at the call with `NoSuchMethodError`, as `pr!!` for `opr (x: T)!![\T\] : T = x` and `pr = (1, 2)` (ledger row 1056). Write no such call in a compiled program.

(* Under the one library's selection, a reduction that is the else part of a binding if, or the right operand of a conditional operator, compiles. *)
component OneLibraryConditionalReduction
export Executable
import List.{...}

orSum(m: Maybe[\ZZ32\], n: ZZ32): ZZ32 = if x <- m then x else SUM[i <- 0#n] i end

allBelow(flag: Boolean, n: ZZ32): Boolean = flag AND: (BIG AND [i <- 0#n] i < n)

anyAbove(flag: Boolean, n: ZZ32): Boolean = flag OR: (BIG OR [i <- 0#n] i > n)

sameLists(xs: List[\ZZ32\], ys: List[\ZZ32\]): Boolean =
  (|xs| = |ys|) AND: (BIG AND [(a, b) <- xs.zip[\ZZ32\](ys)] a = b)

run(): () = do
  println("REACHED")
  assert(orSum(Nothing[\ZZ32\], 4) = 6, "a reduction as the else part of a binding if")
  assert(allBelow(true, 3), "AND: of a reduction over a range")
  deny(anyAbove(false, 3), "OR: of a reduction over a range")
  assert(sameLists(emptyList[\ZZ32\](), emptyList[\ZZ32\]()), "AND: of a reduction over a zip of lists")
  println("PASS")
end

end
# The program whose binding if takes a reduction as its else part, and whose conditional operators take one as their right operand, compiled under the one library's selection, runs: it fails after REACHED while the closure in the generic generate of the index-value pairs of a zip of lists, called through a generator, holds self at the generator's type.
tests=OneLibraryConditionalReduction
run
run_out_contains=REACHED

116:Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library, and a run test there needs the jars of its fourteen components. Run the tests in one of these ways:
117-
118-- `ant testOneLibrary` compiles the fourteen first, with `OneLibraryComponents.test`, in its own caches folder, `ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary`. Each suite deletes that folder when it starts, and only `testFast` and `testOneLibrary` fill it again.
119-- With `junit.sh`, set `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ONE_JVM=1`, and name `OneLibraryComponents.test` first. The compiles write to `default_repository/caches-one`, and the jars stay there after the call. Its `FortressLibrary` alone takes about 135 to 160 s, so run the call in the background (`session.md`).
